lines.text: Some ideas changed the world so completely that we no longer notice them. From the wheel to the chatbot, these are the inventions that made everyday life.
It starts with a turning disc. Around 3500 BCE wheels spun for potters and then rolled under carts, and soon they spread right across Eurasia.
In ancient China, farmers sowed with a seed drill, laying seed in neat rows at an even depth. Europe would build its own versions far later.
Also in China came paper, pressed from plant fibres. Carried along the trade routes to the Islamic world and Europe, it changed writing and learning.
Meanwhile, in the Greek world, someone built a bronze machine of many gears that modelled the Sun and Moon. Nothing like it appears for over a thousand years.
Chinese alchemists searching for an elixir of life found something else: gunpowder. It brought fireworks, then guns and cannon, and changed warfare everywhere.
A magnetised needle that points north was first used in China for fortune-telling, then for finding the way at sea.
Around the same time Bi Sheng printed with movable clay type, pieces that could be arranged and used again. Korean printers later cast it in metal.
In late thirteenth century Italy, lenses held before the eyes let scholars keep reading and working for many more years.
In Germany, Gutenberg's press made books cheap enough for many to own, and helped carry the Renaissance, the Reformation and new science across Europe.
Around 1590 Dutch lens makers built the first microscope. Through it, Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek would discover cells and microbes.
John Harington described an early flush toilet for Queen Elizabeth the first. With sewers, it became a cornerstone of public health.
Then lenses turned to the sky. Galileo's improved telescope soon showed moons circling Jupiter.
In 1656 Christiaan Huygens built a clock kept steady by a swinging pendulum, so accurate that minutes and seconds began to matter.
The steam engine gave power that needed no muscle, wind or water. Improved by James Watt, it drove the Industrial Revolution.
In 1800 Alessandro Volta stacked metal discs and wet cloth into a pile, the first battery, and a steady electric current was born.
A decade later the tin can was patented, letting food keep for years.
Karl Drais's running machine of 1817 led, through pedals and the chain, to the safety bicycle, cheap transport for millions.
The sewing machine stitched far faster than any hand, and helped create factories of ready-made clothes.
With the electric telegraph, news that once took days to cross a continent arrived in minutes. Modern telecommunication had begun.
In 1839 France announced the daguerreotype, a sharp picture on a silvered plate, and the age of portrait photography began.
In 1853 Elisha Otis showed a safety brake that kept a lift from falling, and the skyscraper became possible.
Louis Pasteur found that gentle heating kills harmful microbes in milk and wine, and made milk far safer to drink.
Alfred Nobel invented dynamite, and the fortune it made him still pays for the Nobel Prizes.
The typewriter of 1868 gave us the QWERTY keyboard, and typewriters filled offices for a century.
In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone, carrying the human voice along a wire into homes and offices.
A year later Edison's phonograph recorded sound and played it back. Recorded music had begun.
Around 1879 Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison each made a practical light bulb, a glowing filament that lit the night.
In 1886 Karl Benz patented his three-wheeled motor car with a petrol engine, often called the first practical automobile.
An early zip fastener was patented in 1893, though it took another twenty years to make it work well on clothes.
From the 1890s Marconi sent wireless messages ever further. By the early twenties, radio was broadcasting to the public.
In 1895 Wilhelm Roentgen found rays that pass through flesh but not bone. Within months doctors were using them.
The first vacuum cleaner was a big petrol machine pulled up to the house. Electric ones for the home soon followed.
In 1902 Willis Carrier cooled a printing plant with the first modern air conditioning. In time it made hot cities livable.
In December 1903, at Kitty Hawk, the Wright brothers flew a powered aeroplane under control. The longest flight that day lasted under a minute.
Leo Baekeland invented Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, moulded into telephones, radios and switches.
An electric washing machine of 1908 began to free households from hours of washing by hand.
The Haber process pulled nitrogen from the air to make ammonia for fertiliser, and helped feed a far larger world.
Home refrigerators went on sale in the 1910s, and with food keeping longer, shopping and cooking changed.
In the late twenties, moving pictures were sent through the air. Television became the shared screen of homes around the world.
In 1928 a mould on a lab dish killed the bacteria around it. Penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic, would save countless lives.
At DuPont a team led by Wallace Carothers made nylon, the first fully synthetic fibre, for toothbrushes, stockings and parachutes.
In the late thirties Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany each built a jet engine.
Laszlo Biro, inspired by fast-drying newspaper ink, made a reliable ballpoint pen in Argentina, and the fountain pen gave way.
Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar melting by a radar tube, and the microwave oven was the result.
In December 1947 Bell Labs built the first transistor, a tiny switch that replaced the vacuum tube and sits in every chip today.
The barcode was patented in 1952, though it took more than twenty years before the first product was scanned in a shop.
In 1954 Bell Labs made the first practical silicon solar cell, turning sunlight straight into electricity.
George de Mestral saw burrs clinging to his dog's fur and invented Velcro, now on shoes, bags and even spacecraft.
In 1958 Jack Kilby put a whole circuit on one piece of semiconductor, and Robert Noyce soon made it practical. The microchip was here.
Two years later Theodore Maiman built the first laser, a narrow beam of pure light now used in surgery, scanning and fibre optics.
The contraceptive pill, approved in the United States in 1960, gave women a reliable way to plan their families.
In 1962 a semiconductor first glowed red. The LED now lights almost every lamp, screen and torch.
In 1975 Kodak built a camera that stored pictures as numbers. Digital cameras replaced film, then disappeared into our phones.
Satellites launched for the American military became GPS, which now guides phones, cars, ships and planes.
Touchscreens served shops and kiosks for decades before phones made touch the way most people use a computer.
3D printing builds solid objects layer by layer from a computer design, now used in factories, homes and hospitals.
In 1991 Sony sold the first lithium-ion battery, which now powers our phones, laptops and electric cars.
That same year Tim Berners-Lee's web of linked pages went public from CERN, and became how most people use the internet.
In 2007 Apple's iPhone put a full web browser and a touchscreen in a pocket, and turned the phone into a computer.
In 2012 scientists showed that CRISPR, borrowed from bacteria, could cut DNA at chosen places, opening the way to treat inherited disease.
In 2020 the first mRNA vaccines were approved against COVID-19, teaching the body to recognise a virus from a set of instructions.
And in 2022 ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in about two months, setting off a race to build AI assistants.
From a turning wheel to a talking machine, each invention opened the door to the next.
